items.followUp: State three differences between plant and animal cells.

rubric.why: The student distinguishes the presence of a membrane-bound nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for stating that prokaryotes lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus while eukaryotes have one.

rubric.why: Membrane-bound organelles are a key distinction between the cell types.
rubric.how: Award for contrasting the absence of membrane-bound organelles in prokaryotes with their presence in eukaryotes.

rubric.why: Typical cell size is a textbook difference.
rubric.how: Award for identifying prokaryotic cells as generally smaller and eukaryotic cells as generally larger.

rubric.why: The form of the genetic material is a valid distinction.
rubric.how: Award for stating that prokaryotic DNA is generally circular and eukaryotic chromosomes are linear.

rubric.why: Their typical modes of cell division differ.
rubric.how: Award for stating that prokaryotes divide by binary fission and eukaryotic cells divide by mitosis or meiosis.

modelAnswer: Prokaryotic cells lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells contain them.
Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller; eukaryotic cells are generally larger.
Prokaryotic DNA is generally circular; eukaryotic chromosomes are linear.
Prokaryotes divide by binary fission; eukaryotic cells divide by mitosis or meiosis.

items.followUp: Define zoology and state the language origins of the word zoology.

rubric.why: This gives the meaning of biology.
rubric.how: Award for defining biology as the study or science of life or living organisms.

rubric.why: The word's Greek roots identify its origin.
rubric.how: Award for stating that biology comes from the Greek words bios (life) and logos (study).

modelAnswer: Biology is the scientific study of life and living organisms.
The word biology is derived from the Greek words bios, meaning life, and logos, meaning study.

items.followUp: Give one example each of a micromolecule and a macromolecule.

rubric.why: The question asks for the two classes of biomolecules; textbooks may classify them by size or by chemical nature.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for correctly naming both classes: micromolecules and macromolecules, or inorganic and organic molecules.

modelAnswer: Biomolecules are classified as micromolecules and macromolecules.

items.followUp: Write two characteristics of a scientific theory.

rubric.why: A hypothesis must be testable through investigation.
rubric.description: State that a hypothesis is testable.
rubric.how: Award for saying that a hypothesis can be tested, for example by an experiment.

rubric.why: A hypothesis is a provisional explanation based on available observations.
rubric.description: State that a hypothesis is tentative and explanatory.
rubric.how: Award for describing it as a tentative or proposed explanation, or one based on observations.

modelAnswer: A hypothesis is a tentative explanation for observations.
It must be testable through investigation or experimentation.

items.followUp: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative observations?

rubric.why: Quantitative observations report measured or counted quantities.
rubric.description: Identify the numerical basis of quantitative observations.
rubric.how: Award for stating that quantitative observations use numbers, counts, or measurements.

rubric.why: Numerical measurements are more precise and easier to compare than descriptions alone.
rubric.description: Explain why quantitative observations are more accurate.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that numerical measurements are precise, objective, or readily compared and repeated.

modelAnswer: Quantitative observations are expressed as numbers or measurements.
They are generally more accurate because they are precise and can be compared objectively, unlike descriptive qualitative observations.

items.followUp: What type of genetic material is found in a viroid, and what makes a prion unusual?

rubric.why: A prion is an infectious protein particle.
rubric.how: Award for identifying prions as infectious proteins or infectious protein particles.

rubric.why: Viroids are infectious RNA molecules without a protein coat.
rubric.how: Award for identifying viroids as small infectious RNA molecules, typically without a protein coat.

modelAnswer: Viroids are small infectious RNA molecules that lack a protein coat.

items.followUp: Define cell division and give one example of an organism that can regenerate.

rubric.why: Regeneration involves the regrowth or replacement of lost body parts.
rubric.how: Award for defining regeneration as the ability to regrow or replace lost body parts.

rubric.why: In some organisms, regeneration can produce a whole organism from a body fragment; examples may illustrate this.
rubric.description: State the outcome or an example of regeneration.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a fragment can grow into a whole organism, or giving a suitable example such as Planaria or starfish.

modelAnswer: Regeneration is the ability of an organism to regrow or replace lost body parts.
In some organisms, a body fragment can develop into a complete organism, as in Planaria.

items.followUp: What happens to the chromosomes during mitosis?

rubric.why: S is the synthesis phase of interphase.
rubric.how: Award for identifying S phase as the synthesis phase of the cell cycle.

rubric.why: DNA is copied during S phase, duplicating each chromosome.
rubric.description: State what happens during S phase.
rubric.how: Award for stating that DNA replicates or is copied, so each chromosome is duplicated.

modelAnswer: S phase is the synthesis phase of interphase.
During this phase, DNA replicates and each chromosome is duplicated.
